title: If you saw it, which side do you land on? #broadway #westend #tonyawa...
transcript: Why is there a debate about whether this 2,000 year old play is new or a revival? So much so, in fact, that the Tony Awards considered it a revival, while the outer critics circle considered it a new play. Essentially, this is a new take on Oedipus, originally by Sophocles, but re contextualized for modern day in this new adaptation by Robert Icke. I actually think there's a case to be made both ways here. The main case for calling it a revival, even though it's a new adaptation, is that it's following in a very long tradition of old classic plays that were written in other languages originally getting revived in a new “version.” Essentially, when you see a revival of Ibsen, Chekhov, Strindberg, and in this case, the ancient Greek plays, you're almost never gonna see a literal, direct translation of it (onstage) What they do is they give that literal translation to a playwright, Who kind of runs it through their own writerly filter. And the industry standard, at least in the U S. And London, is that it's still considered a revival because the playwright is sticking pretty closely to the blueprint of the original play. And this has been pretty consistently true. But we saw it most recently, for example, with Amy Herzog's new versions of enemy of the people and a Doll's House, Heidi Schrek's version of Uncle Vanya and many, many more. So a case could be made that Robert Icke is basically following in that same tradition, and therefore it should be considered a revival. However, his adaptation of Oedipus deviates from the original more than any of the examples I just named. I can speak from experience that I've seen many of these different versions of Uncle Vanya or the Seagull, and to be honest, without a side by side comparison, I can barely tell the difference. They make some cuts, they add bits of dialogue here and there, and make interpretative choices about how to express the sentiments of the characters in their voice. Maybe there's bigger differences that I'm just not perceptive enough to pick up on, but in either case, it's pretty clear contrast to what Robert Icke did. Like, they're usually not adding characters into the play that weren't in the original. These other revivals might, use some modern parlance, put the actors in modern clothes, but rarely will the script itself overtly incorporate elements of modern society and technology. So that's the argument for considering it a new play. Having said that, I think a lot of people felt, despite all of the changes that he made to transplant the setting, the feel of it, the flow and structure of the story, the major themes of it, the dramatic beats, and the general experience of watching this drama play out still felt at its core, like you were watching what Sophocles wrote. Yes, he adapted it more than Amy Herzog adapted enemy of The people. But he didn't adapt it as much as, say, James Ijames did with Fat Ham. Normally I would have a strong opinion on this either way, but this is a very rare case where I genuinely think either interpretation is valid.
classificationReason: Discussion is analytical/intellectual commentary on the debate over whether Robert Icke's adaptation counts as a revival or new play (Tony Awards vs. Outer Critics Circle), not a first-hand review of attending the production.
